title: R-based workflow to estimate chilling requirements in multiple fruit tree genotypes using Partial Least Squares regression: Prunus armeniaca L. case☆
author: Muñoz-Morales, Ortuño-Hernández, et al.

steps.title: Set up R environment
steps.instruction: Install and load the chillR package (version 0.76) and any other required R libraries, then clone or download the GitHub repository https://github.com/CEBASFruitBreed/R-workflow-ChillPLS containing the code and dataset.

steps.title: List genotype Excel files
steps.instruction: Generate a list of all Excel files in the "Genotypes/" directory that match the required naming pattern.

steps.title: Read and preprocess each file
steps.instruction: Iterate over the file list: read each Excel file, keep its base name, remove the columns named group1 and group2, convert the Year column to integer type and the pheno column to a factor.

steps.title: Run PLS regression
steps.instruction: Apply the PLS_chill_force function to each pre‑processed dataset using the pre‑processed climate data; set split_month = 11 so that the dormant season starts in November; calculate chilling accumulation with the three models – Chilling Hours, Utah Model, and Dynamic Model (recommended).

steps.title: Save PLS results
steps.instruction: Write the output of each PLS analysis to a new Excel file in the folder "Genotypes/Results_PLS_Genotypes/" using the original source filename for traceability.

steps.title: Export genotype group subsets
steps.instruction: For each genotype, extract group identifiers from the Cultivar column, split the data into subsets defined by each unique group combination, and export each subset as an individual Excel file.

steps.title: Identify chilling period (process_PLS_file)
steps.instruction: Run the process_PLS_file function on each dataset: keep rows where model coefficients are negative and VIP scores are ≥ 0.8, retrieve the genotype identifier, define the chilling period as the first and last day of the filtered rows, restrict the end of chill accumulation to at most one day before the genotype’s median bloom date, compile all genotypes into a single data frame and export it as an Excel file.

steps.title: Apply process_PLS_file to progenies
steps.instruction: Retrieve the lists of Excel files containing Chill Portions data for the two apricot progenies ‘BxC’ and ‘GxC’ from their respective directories, apply process_PLS_file to each list, and save the resulting chilling‑period files as separate Excel files.

steps.title: Calculate temperature metrics (process_Jday)
steps.instruction: For each genotype, determine the starting Julian day (Start_JDay) from the daily values, process the corresponding hourly temperature data with the stack_hourly_temps function, apply tempResponse to estimate chilling responses for the Chilling Hours, Utah, and Dynamic models, store the results in a structured list, and export individual Excel files named with the genotype and group ID.

steps.title: Create final compiled chill metrics
steps.instruction: Use the process_final_file function to read all phenological Excel files, filter to the predefined seasons of interest, extract a year‑based suffix to identify each season, assign the genotype based on the file name, reshape the data with pivot tables to generate separate columns for each season containing Chill Hours, Chill Units and Chill Portions, then compile all files and save the combined result as a single final Excel file.

steps.title: Generate overall summary output
steps.instruction: In the final workflow step, read all Excel files from the specified directories, filter the relevant data, extract seasonal chilling metrics, compile the results, and produce a final output file for each genotype that summarizes Chill Hours, Chill Units and Chill Portions across all seasons.

description: Following this introduction, we present the code and workflow used in our case study. The code, written in the R programming language, outlines the essential steps required to generate the outputs and is accompanied by a brief explanation of the results and their implications. All dormancy-related metrics, including the PLS regression analysis and the calculation of CR using the three most common chill models, are implemented in the chillR package (version 0.76) [11]. The complete code and dataset used in the analyses described below are freely available in the following GitHub repository (https://github.com/CEBASFruitBreed/R-workflow-ChillPLS). In fruit tree breeding, phenotyping is often a major bottleneck, especially for traits linked to dormancy release and flowering. Determining cultivar-specific CR is particularly important, since this trait defines cultivar adaptability to specific climates under current and future conditions. Traditionally, CRs are estimated using the forcing shoots method, which involves collecting dormant shoots during winter and placing them under controlled conditions (20–25 °C) to induce bud break. Although widely used, this approach is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and unsuitable for large breeding populations. The methodology presented here provides an efficient alternative, allowing breeders to rapidly process and analyze extensive phenological datasets and generate standardized CR values for downstream applications (Fig. 3).Fig. 3Graphical summary of the workflow, showing input files (flowering and climate data in Excel files), intermediate steps (preprocessing and PLS regression analysis), and the final outputs (genotype-specific chilling requirement estimates).Fig. 3 The outputs generated in this study have several potential applications, including QTL mapping, which relies on precise phenotypic data across segregating populations such as those evaluated in this study (BxC’ and ‘GxC’).
